notes:
I've put together notes for most of Amos 9, but the coverage is uneven. Searching and fetching ran out before I could read the commentaries on individual verses for vv. 2–6, 8–10 and 12–14. For those verses the notes rest mainly on Enduring Word and on short excerpts that turned up in search results.

**What I couldn't find:**
- **Catholic and Orthodox readings:** nothing from newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org came up, so that section is missing.
- **Modern scholarship:** nothing from bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org. The only scholarly views below come second-hand through StudyLight and Precept Austin.
- **Prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching:** no sources found.
- **Lutheran, Pentecostal and Anglican teachers:** none of their own writers turned up.
- **Tradition labels:** I only name a tradition where the page itself gives one. StudyLight labels Clarke as Wesleyan/Methodist, Coffman as Restoration Movement and Chuck Smith as Calvary Chapel/dispensationalist.

The two places where the commentators really split are v. 1 (which altar is meant) and vv. 11–15 (whether the promises are fulfilled in the church or still await a future national Israel).

---

**v. 1**
- **Traditional reading:** This is the fifth and last of Amos's visions, which began in 7:1. Precept Austin notes that an altar normally means mercy through a substitute sacrifice. When altar and sacrifice are despised, the altar becomes a place of judgment only. https://www.preceptaustin.org/amos-9-commentary
- Guzik (Enduring Word) says the threshold is often the strongest part of a building. So the shaking pictures total destruction, and God is shown supervising the judgment himself, not standing apart from it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-9/
- **Where commentators differ: which altar?**
  - *Bethel:* Constable thinks the altar at Bethel is probably in view since Bethel was the worship site in view in most of this book. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/9-1.html Barnes and Matthew Henry also place it at Jeroboam's idolatrous altar at Bethel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/amos/9-1.htm
  - *Jerusalem:* Calvin argues for the true temple, because had God appeared in Dan or Bethel, it would have been an indirect approbation of superstition. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/9-1.html Keil and Delitzsch point out that Bethel had several altars (3:14). They conclude this is the altar of burnt offering in Jerusalem, and they read the command as symbolic, not as the literal destruction of a temple. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/amos-9.html
  - *Coffman (Restoration Movement)* also rejects Bethel. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/9-1.html
  - *Clarke (Methodist)* suggests it may be one of the altars at Dan or Beersheba. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/9-1.html
  - *Pulpit Commentary:* its exposition section says Jerusalem, but its homiletics section says Bethel. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/amos-9.html
- **Other view:** McComiskey (quoted by Precept Austin) reads the temple as a picture of the northern kingdom's religion as a whole, not a literal building. https://www.preceptaustin.org/amos-9-commentary

**vv. 2–4**
- Guzik's summary: Israel could run but not hide. Neither Sheol, heaven, Carmel nor the sea could shield them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-9/
- Guzik ties "for harm and not for good" (v. 4) to the covenant curses for chronic disobedience in Deuteronomy 28 and Leviticus 26. He contrasts this with the new covenant, where "God is for us" (Romans 8:31). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-9/

**vv. 5–6**
- Guzik says the title "Lord GOD" is used 12 times in chapters 7–9 to stress God's sovereignty. He adds that the prophets keep basing what we should do on who God is. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-9/
- Quoting Hubbard, Guzik notes that v. 6 is hard to translate. The heavenly structure might be a "staircase" or a "roof-chamber." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-9/

**v. 7**
- **Traditional reading:** Ellicott says Israel had presumed on God's special favour, and Amos asks whether they are any safer than the Ethiopians they looked down on. https://biblehub.com/amos/9-7.htm The Pulpit Commentary says Israel's election would not save them unless their conduct matched God's choice. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/amos/9-7.htm
- Precept Austin notes the Cushites lived in what is now southern Egypt and Sudan, and Israel thought of them as living at the "end of the earth." https://www.preceptaustin.org/amos-9-commentary
- Several sources identify Caphtor with Crete. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/amos/9-7.htm
- **A rejected reading:** Some had taken the comparison to mean Israel, like the Ethiopian, had not "changed its skin," i.e. its character. Calvin reject[ed] as strained that idea. Barnes leaned toward a version of it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/9-7.html

**vv. 8–10**
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik says the exile would sift Israel to purify it, not to wipe it out. Only "the sinners of My people" who presume on God fall under judgment. He quotes Spurgeon comforting believers that the farmer is not angry with his wheat when he shakes it in the sieve. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-9/
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say the kingdom would perish, but the house of Jacob would not as individuals. Not even the least of the righteous would fall. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/amos-9.html
- **Scholarship:** Coffman reports that some scholars treat v. 8b as a later addition by a Judean editor. He rejects that view firmly. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/amos-9.html

**v. 11** (where commentators differ most)
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik says the shift from v. 10 to v. 11 is the book's most abrupt. He calls "tabernacle" a humble word for David's house: the dynasty had sunk so low it could no longer be called a house. He sees it fulfilled in Jesus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-9/
- Calvin read it as God restoring David's royal dignity after a time when the house was like a "mean cottage." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/9-11.html
- **Reading 1: fulfilled in Christ and the church**
  - Keil and Delitzsch say this harmonizes with James's use of the verse in Acts 15. There it shows that believing Gentiles were received without circumcision. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/amos/9-11.htm
  - Matthew Henry says that in the gospel church God's tabernacle was set up again. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Amo/Amo_009.cfm
  - Coffman (Restoration Movement) reads it as a prophecy of the church and denies that it refers to David's dynasty. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/9-11.html
  - Gill applies it to Christ and also to a later reviving of a decayed church. Precept Austin criticises this as too non-literal. https://www.preceptaustin.org/amos_commentaries
- **Reading 2: a future, literal Davidic kingdom (dispensational)**
  - Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) takes it as the Davidic kingdom God will raise up again. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/9-11.html
  - Henry Morris says it will be fulfilled at Christ's second coming. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62072/
  - Feinberg argues that James's quotation does not warrant us in holding, as some do, that this prophecy is fulfilled completely in this age of grace. https://www.preceptaustin.org/amos-9-commentary
  - GotQuestions sees a restoration of the Jewish nation in the end times, and possibly a tabernacle like David's during the millennium. https://www.gotquestions.org/tabernacle-of-David.html
- **Scholarship:** Coffman cites a view that the verses assume the dynasty had already ended, which would date them after 586 BC. He rejects it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/amos-9.html The Expositor's Bible notes that vv. 11–15 are by many denied to Amos. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/amos.html Criswell answers that prophets naturally follow condemnation with hope. https://www.preceptaustin.org/amos-9-commentary

**v. 12**
- Guzik explains why Acts 15:17 says "the rest of mankind" instead of "the remnant of Edom." The Greek Septuagint read "Edom" as "Adam," meaning mankind. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-9/
- The Gospel Coalition's commentary on Amos says James saw the verse fulfilled in preaching the gospel to Gentiles and their inclusion in the church. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/amos/
- Constable says James used it to show Gentiles did not need circumcision or the Mosaic Law. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/amos-9.html

**v. 13**
- Guzik says the plowman and reaper "bump into each other" because the crops are so plentiful, yet the people still have work to do. He quotes Spurgeon that increased activity among God's workers is a sign of revival. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-9/
- Keil and Delitzsch say the second half of the verse is taken from Joel 3:18. It echoes the "land flowing with milk and honey." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/amos/9-15.htm

**v. 14**
- Keil and Delitzsch see a reversal of the curse in Amos 5:11: no more building houses that others live in. They take the Hebrew phrase as "turning misfortune into prosperity," not literally coming back from captivity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/amos/9-15.htm
- Guzik contrasts Jeroboam II's prosperity, which was not "in the LORD," with prosperity that comes from God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-9/

**v. 15** (commentators differ)
- **Both sides agree on one point:** the return from Babylon did not fulfil "never again." Calvin and D.A. Carson (TGC) both note this. https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/comment3/comm_vol27/htm/iv.ix.xii.htm and https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/devotionals/read-the-bible/1-chronicles-15-james-2-amos-9-luke-4/
- **Reading 1: the church**
  - The Pulpit Commentary says the promise must be taken of the spiritual seed, planted in God's land, the Church of Christ. https://biblehub.com/amos/9-15.htm
  - Barnes says that as the true Israel spread to all nations, the whole earth became "the land." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/amos/9-15.htm
  - Keil and Delitzsch reject both the post-exile return and a future Jewish return to Palestine as the fulfilment. They see it in the church through the ages. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/amos/9-15.htm
- **Reading 2: a future national return**
  - Gill saw the prophecy as still to come, because the Jews were later uprooted by the Romans. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/n84/amos/9-15.html
  - Clarke (Methodist) says it has not yet been fulfilled, it therefore follows that it will and must be fulfilled. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/niv/amos/9-15.html
- **Popular modern teaching:** A Bible Hub Q&A article connects the verse to the founding of the modern State of Israel. It rejects "replacement" readings. https://biblehub.com/q/Amos_9_15_s_link_to_modern_Israel.htm
- **Summary of the options:** Constable notes that amillennialists find the fulfilment in the return from exile, in the church spiritually, or in heaven. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/amos-9.html
